Content:
In this lesson, we will generalize Bayes' theorem to deal with situations where the sample space [MATH: \mathcal S] is partitioned into a disjoint union of multiple events.

Content:
Suppose we have three events [MATH: A_1,A_2,] and [MATH: A_3] that form a disjoint union of the sample space [MATH: \mathcal S,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/451c3823846faf151b85fc6f353e93be]

Content:
Now consider an event [MATH: B] that also lies in the sample space:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d6f7f5c1be0cb59f3f9dfb6709179275]

Content:
Bayes' theorem states that

Content:
[MATH: P(A_1|B)=\dfrac{P(B|A_1)P(A_1)}{P(B)}.]

Content:
Now, the law of total probability tells us that

Content:
[MATH: P(B)=P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3).]

Content:
Substituting this into Bayes' theorem, we get

Content:
[MATH: P(A_1 | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_1) P(A_1)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)} .]

Content:
Using similar arguments, we can say that for [MATH: A_k] for [MATH: k=1,2,3,] we have

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)}]

Content:
which is usually written more compactly as

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^3 P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}.]

Content:
It's easy to see how this generalizes. If the disjoint union [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n] covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}]

Content:
Let's see an example of how to apply this theorem.

If the disjoint union [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n] covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}]

where [MATH: k=1,2,\ldots,n.]

In our case, [MATH: n=3,] and [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3] covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

[MATH: P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) = 1.]

As a result,

[MATH: P(A_{1})|= 1 − (P(A_{2}) + P(A_{3})); = 1 − (0.3 + 0.4); = 0.3.]

Therefore,

[MATH: P(A_{1}|B)|= (P(B|A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(∑_(i = 1)^(3)P(B|A_{i})P(A_{i})); = (P(B|A_{1})P(A_{1}))/(P(B|A_{1})P(A_{1}) + P(B|A_{2})P(A_{2}) + P(B|A_{3})P(A_{3})); = ((0.23)(0.3))/((0.23)(0.3) + (0.26)(0.3) + (0.18)(0.4)); = (0.069)/(0.219); ≈ 0.315.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: C] be the event that a customer travels with children, [MATH: B] be the event that a customer takes the bus, and [MATH: I_1, I_2, I_3] be the event that a customer chooses itinerary [MATH: 1,] [MATH: 2,] or [MATH: 3,] respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

  • From the bullet points, we have the following information: [MATH: P(I_{1}) = 0.25|P(B|I_{1}) = 0.6; P(I_{2}) = 0.3|P(B|I_{2}) = 0.3; P(I_{3}) = 0.45|P(B|I_{3}) = 0.2] The disjoint union [MATH: I_1 \sqcup I_2 \sqcup I_3] covers the entire sample space, and we have [MATH: P(I_1)+ P(I_2) + P(I_3) = 0.25+0.3+0.45 = 1.]

  • Since [MATH: 65\%] of customers have children, we have [MATH: P(C) = 0.65.]

  • Since [MATH: 40\%] of customers with children choose the bus, we have [MATH: P(B | C) = 0.4.]

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen customer that chooses the bus travels with children, which is represented as [MATH: P(C | B).]

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

[MATH: P(C|B)|= (P(B|C)P(C))/(P(B)); = (P(B|C)P(C))/(P(B|I_{1})P(I_{1}) + P(B|I_{2})P(I_{2}) + P(B|I_{3})P(I_{3})); = ((0.4)(0.65))/((0.6)(0.25) + (0.3)(0.3) + (0.2)(0.45)); = (0.26)/(0.33); ≈ 0.788,]

rounded to [MATH: 3] decimal places.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will generalize Bayes' theorem to deal with situations where the sample space [MATH: \mathcal S] is partitioned into a disjoint union of multiple events.

Content:
Suppose we have three events [MATH: A_1,A_2,] and [MATH: A_3] that form a disjoint union of the sample space [MATH: \mathcal S,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/451c3823846faf151b85fc6f353e93be]

Content:
Now consider an event [MATH: B] that also lies in the sample space:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d6f7f5c1be0cb59f3f9dfb6709179275]

Content:
Bayes' theorem states that

Content:
[MATH: P(A_1|B)=\dfrac{P(B|A_1)P(A_1)}{P(B)}.]

Content:
Now, the law of total probability tells us that

Content:
[MATH: P(B)=P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3).]

Content:
Substituting this into Bayes' theorem, we get

Content:
[MATH: P(A_1 | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_1) P(A_1)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)} .]

Content:
Using similar arguments, we can say that for [MATH: A_k] for [MATH: k=1,2,3,] we have

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B|A_1)P(A_1) + P(B|A_2)P(A_2) + P(B|A_3)P(A_3)}]

Content:
which is usually written more compactly as

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^3 P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}.]

Content:
It's easy to see how this generalizes. If the disjoint union [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n] covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

Content:
[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}]

Content:
Let's see an example of how to apply this theorem.

[MATH: P(B|A_{1}) = 0.23,; P(B|A_{2}) = 0.26,|P(A_{2}) = 0.3; P(B|A_{3}) = 0.18,|P(A_{3}) = 0.4]

Explanation:
If the disjoint union [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup \ldots \sqcup A_n] covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

[MATH: P(A_k | B) = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{P(B)} = \dfrac{P(B|A_k) P(A_k)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(B|A_i)P(A_i)}]

where [MATH: k=1,2,\ldots,n.]

In our case, [MATH: n=3,] and [MATH: A_1 \sqcup A_2 \sqcup A_3] covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

[MATH: P(A_1) + P(A_2) + P(A_3) = 1.]

As a result,

[MATH: P(A_{1})|= 1 − (P(A_{2}) + P(A_{3})); = 1 − (0.3 + 0.4); = 0.3.]
